tldr: A visuo-tactile world model that unifies camera views, tactile images, marker displacements, and task state onto a single canvas. By training with a pretrained video generative model and three consistency reward models, it enables accurate policy evaluation and reinforcement learning without running real robots.
hero_caption: Overall overview and key results of PhysCanvas. By tiling heterogeneous modalities such as multi-view cameras and touch into a single canvas and predicting them with a video model, it achieves real-robot-free closed-loop evaluation (improving the correlation with real success rates from 0.602 to 0.885) and policy improvement via GRPO (boosting success rates from 59.1% to 70.8%).
overview:
When robots learn and evaluate complex contact-rich tasks (like unscrewing caps or inserting test tubes), running physical hardware repeatedly takes substantial time, costs money, and risks hardware damage. Action-conditioned world models that simulate environmental changes in response to robot actions have gained attention as interactive simulators. However, conventional video generation-based methods often produce visually plausible rollouts that fail to capture fine contact or slipping, while also producing unreliable task success judgements.

To address this, the authors propose PhysCanvas. Its core idea is bold: instead of building separate networks for touch, it tiles multi-view RGB camera views, optical tactile images, sensor surface marker displacement vectors, and task state onto a single large image canvas with specialized color and pattern encodings. An existing large-scale video generative backbone (Wan 2.2) predicts the entire canvas at once. This lets optical touch directly reuse the rich visual and temporal priors learned by the video model. In addition, to prevent scene collapse, visuo-tactile inconsistencies, and task outcome discrepancies, they introduce consistency-aware post-training guided by three independent frozen reward models.

Evaluated on four real-world dual-arm manipulation tasks, the Pearson correlation between policy success rates inside the generated simulation and in the real world dramatically improved from 0.602 to 0.885. Furthermore, when policies were post-trained with reinforcement learning entirely through imagined rollouts inside this world model, the average real-world success rate improved by 11.7 percentage points, from 59.1% to 70.8%.
contributions: Proposed the Unified Canvas, integrating camera RGB, tactile images, marker displacements, task state, and robot actions into a single image space to directly leverage the expressive power of pretrained video generation backbones without specialized tactile encoders.

Introduced consistency-aware post-training using three reward models monitoring scene preservation (Scene), visual-tactile compatibility (Modality), and agreement with real task outcomes (State) to prevent physical and semantic collapse.

Demonstrated an evaluation pipeline that accurately predicts real-world policy performance via closed-loop rollouts, along with a reinforcement learning (GRPO) framework that improves physical robot success rates purely through imagined trial-and-error.

sections.heading: Building a world model consistent not just in visuals, but in touch and task outcomes
sections.summary: Contact-rich manipulation requires both vision and touch, but conventional video models ignore tactile signals and frequently produce conflicting success judgements. This paper presents PhysCanvas, which unifies all modalities onto a single canvas for joint prediction via a pretrained video backbone, enforcing physical consistency with three reward models.
sections.details:
Evaluating or post-training robot policies purely through real physical interaction is very challenging due to hardware wear and tear and heavy human supervision. Consequently, action-conditioned world models that predict future environmental transitions from robot action commands are actively explored as virtual simulators.

However, in contact-rich tasks like cap unscrewing or test tube insertion, camera images (RGB) alone cannot reliably reveal whether an object is held firmly or slipping. Furthermore, existing visuo-tactile models typically build dedicated encoders for tactile sensors and inject them into video models, requiring pipeline redesign whenever sensor geometry changes. In addition, training solely with pixel-level reconstruction losses produces semantic inconsistencies—such as the tactile sensor signaling a firm grip while the object visibly slips away, or claiming success when an attempt failed. These issues mislead policy evaluation and learning.

To tackle this, the authors posed two questions: (1) Can heterogeneous modalities be unified into a shared visual space without specialized architectures? (2) Can high-level semantics like task success be injected without adding extra networks?

PhysCanvas is their answer. By laying out all observations within the input space of a pretrained video generative AI and teaching physical consistency through reward-guided post-training, they construct a reliable simulator.

These tasks involve rich contact dynamics like reorientation and tight mechanical mating that vision alone cannot fully capture.

sections.heading: Progress in video world models and the remaining hurdle of tactile integration
sections.summary: Action-conditioned video models are advancing rapidly in robotics, but integrating touch has typically required complex pipelines with custom encoders. PhysCanvas sets itself apart by rendering touch and task state directly as image patches, handling everything within a single pretrained video backbone.
sections.details:
### Action-Conditioned World Models in Robotics
Driven by breakthroughs in video diffusion models and Flow Matching, repurposing large pretrained video generators as action-conditioned world models has gained strong momentum. Projecting robot end-effector trajectories directly onto image space has improved spatial controllability. Yet, solving contact-rich tasks requires simulating the tactile signals that policies rely on alongside video.

### Current Visuo-Tactile World Models and Our Positioning
Prior efforts incorporating optical tactile sensors (which image gel surface deformation with internal cameras), such as OmniVTA and FeelWorld, typically use two-stream architectures. They build dedicated tactile VAEs or encoders and connect them to visual models via attention mechanisms. This design complicates the pipeline and limits generalization due to the modest size of tactile datasets.

In contrast, PhysCanvas takes the approach of placing tactile images and marker displacement fields directly onto the canvas as image patches. Because tactile signals also exhibit local spatial correlations, this approach allows touch to directly inherit the powerful spatio-temporal priors acquired by video models trained on large-scale natural imagery.

sections.heading: Drawing everything on one canvas and curbing physical violations with three rewards
sections.summary: PhysCanvas organizes camera views, tactile images, marker displacement, and task state onto a unified grid canvas, predicting future frames with the Wan 2.2 video model conditioned on projected motion images. It then conducts consistency-aware post-training using three frozen reward models for scene preservation, visual-tactile compatibility, and task state.
sections.details:
### 3.1 & 3.2 Unified Multimodal Canvas and Action Conditioning
The authors first observed that a standard video VAE pretrained on natural images (Wan VAE) reconstructs optical tactile images with higher fidelity than a dedicated tactile VAE (UniT) (PSNR 35.51 vs 31.72). Leveraging this, they pack all information into a single RGB canvas.

- **Canvas Layout**: The top row contains three camera RGB views (one static base view and two wrist views), the middle row holds four fingertip tactile images, and the bottom row features marker displacement fields (3D displacement vectors $(x, y, z)$ normalized into RGB channels) and a task state bar (task ID represented by color, success/failure represented by striped textures).
- **Action Conditioning**: Joint position and gripper commands are converted into "Motion Images" by projecting the robot's CAD model (URDF) directly onto camera viewpoints using camera parameters. These motion images are aligned and added (position-wise fusion) to the latent features of the canvas. Action features are deliberately not added to the task state patch, forcing the model to infer task outcomes indirectly through self-attention across image regions.
- **Generative Backbone**: The model employs Wan 2.2 (a 5B-parameter Flow Matching Transformer) to autoregressively predict multimodal futures up to 8 frames ahead, referencing the initial frame of the episode as a visual anchor.

### 3.3 Consistency-Aware Post-Training
Because pixel reconstruction loss (Flow Matching loss) alone cannot prevent long-horizon physical violations, three lightweight frozen reward models (ResNet-18 based) guide simulator fine-tuning:

1. **Scene Reward Model**: Prevents unmanipulated objects or backgrounds from randomly deforming or vanishing by scoring and maximizing similarity with the initial frame.
2. **Modality Reward Model**: Evaluates visual-tactile compatibility (e.g., verifying that tactile signals do not trigger without visual contact) and maximizes the consistency score.
3. **State Reward Model**: Determines whether the task succeeded from the generated camera view. Rather than simply driving success rates upward, it is trained with binary cross-entropy loss against ground-truth labels from real executions, ensuring the model faithfully predicts failures when actions fail.

### 3.4 Application to Policy Evaluation and Reinforcement Learning
With the learned world model, policies can be executed in closed-loop rollouts from an initial image to evaluate performance virtually. Furthermore, within these imagined rollouts, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) can be applied using success rewards from the State Reward Model, improving policy performance without collecting a single additional real-world transition.

sections.heading: Correlation with real success jumps to 0.885, and imagined training lifts success by 11.7%
sections.summary: Across four real tasks, PhysCanvas outperforms existing video baselines in visual quality and action tracking. Consistency post-training boosts the correlation between world-model and real evaluations from 0.602 to 0.885, while imagined RL improves real-world policy success from 59.1% to 70.8%.
sections.details:
### 4.1 & 4.2 Generation Quality and Baseline Comparisons
Experiments were conducted on an ARX AC One dual-arm robot equipped with three cameras and four Xense tactile sensors across four tasks: test tube insertion, bottle cap unscrewing, block sorting, and Rubik's cube manipulation.

- **RGB Generation and Controllability**: Compared against video baselines like EVAC, Open-Sora, and WoVR, PhysCanvas achieved the best scores across PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, FID, and FVD. Notably, end-effector (EEF) tracking error was 0.685 pixels, 51.9% lower than the closest baseline, demonstrating that generated rollouts follow commanded actions with high fidelity.
- **Token Local Integration**: Visualizing token distributions inside the Transformer via t-SNE revealed that shallow layers actively blend information across modalities, while deeper layers gradually separate into modality-specific representations.

### 4.3 Ablation Studies
Removing individual components highlighted their specific contributions:
- Injecting actions as spatially aligned motion images ($\mathcal{M}_1$) improved RGB LPIPS by 58.3% and reduced EEF tracking error by 32.6% compared to global AdaLN injection ($\mathcal{M}_0$).
- Adding the Scene Reward Model ($\mathcal{M}_2$) suppressed background and object drift, improving FVD by 10.4%.
- Adding task state supervision ($\mathcal{M}_3$) improved FID by 26.4%.
- Adding the Modality Reward Model ($\mathcal{M}_4$) reduced contact MAE from 0.02491 to 0.02278 along with marker displacement errors, eliminating visual-tactile discrepancies.

### 4.4 Reliability as a Policy Evaluation Simulator
Three policy types—ACT, Flow Matching (FM), and $\pi_{0.5}$—were rolled out in the world model and compared against real-world performance. Without task state supervision ($\mathcal{M}_2$), the Pearson correlation between simulated and real success was 0.602. With full supervision ($\mathcal{M}_3$), it jumped to 0.885 ($R^2$ rose from 0.413 to 0.791). This confirms high reliability: policies that succeed in simulation also succeed on the physical robot.

### 4.5 Real-World Policy Improvement via Imagined RL
Policies explored inside the world model and updated via GRPO using judgements from the State Reward Model. As a result, the average real-world success rate of the pretrained $\pi_{0.5}$ policy increased from the SFT baseline of 59.1% to 67.5% with basic world model training ($\mathcal{M}_1$), and reached 70.8% (+11.7 percentage points) with the full consistency-trained model ($\mathcal{M}_4$). Gains were particularly pronounced on block sorting (+6.6 pt) and Rubik's cube manipulation (+10.0 pt).

captions.F6: Responsiveness to action interventions. When a command to open the gripper is injected while lifting a block, the predicted video (Pred) correctly shows the block falling, and the fingertip tactile response disappears. This confirms the model learns causal physical contact dynamics rather than mere visual transitions.
captions.F7: Effects of consistency losses. (Left) Without the Scene Reward Model, objects like the test tube rack deform over time, whereas adding it preserves the initial layout. (Right) Without the Modality Reward Model, tactile responses over-activate during Rubik's cube rotation (red box), while adding it restricts touch to correct, localized contact.

sections.heading: The promise of canvas-based visuo-tactile unification
sections.summary: PhysCanvas demonstrates that heterogeneous modalities can be modeled simply and accurately using a unified visual canvas and three consistency rewards. It marks a significant step forward in showing that multimodal world models can serve as powerful simulators for policy evaluation and improvement without physical hardware.
sections.details:
This study demonstrates that non-visual information like touch and task state, when converted into suitable visual representations and tiled on a single canvas, can fully leverage the priors of state-of-the-art video generative models. A single generator can achieve physically consistent simulation without adding dedicated tactile encoders.

Furthermore, the work shows that regularizing higher-level semantics—scene preservation, modality compatibility, and task outcomes—via reward models is essential for building a reliable simulator, beyond basic pixel-level training. This opens up safe, low-cost policy evaluation and provides a viable route to boosting real-robot success rates directly through reinforcement learning in imagination.

sections.heading: Appendix: Real hardware setup and the mechanics of imagined GRPO
sections.summary: Details on the dual-arm robotic system with four optical tactile sensors, the RGB encoding scheme for marker displacement fields, and the mathematical formulation of dual-clip GRPO inside the world model.
sections.details:
### Hardware and Sensor Configuration
Experiments used an ARX AC One dual-arm robot (6 DoF plus gripper per arm). Three cameras were set up: one static base view and two wrist cameras (each at $224\times 224$ resolution). Four Xense optical tactile sensors were mounted on the fingertips, fully synchronized at 10 Hz. Each sensor tracks 700 markers ($35\times 20$ grid). The 3D displacement vectors $(\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z)$ from the initial episode state are clipped to $[-0.06, 0.06]$, normalized into RGB channels, and embedded onto the canvas.

### GRPO Algorithm Inside the World Model
For imagined reinforcement learning, 8 trajectory candidates are sampled as a group from a single initial state using stochastic policy transitions (Flow-SDE). The final frame of each rollout is evaluated by the frozen State Reward Model, granting reward 1 if the success probability $p_i^{\mathrm{end}} \ge 0.5$, and 0 otherwise. Because advantages $A_i$ are normalized by the group mean and standard deviation, groups where all 8 rollouts succeed or fail provide no learning signal and are automatically skipped.
Policy updates employ asymmetric PPO clipping ($[0.8, 1.28]$) alongside dual clipping, which caps the surrogate objective at $-c A_i$ ($c=3.0$) for negative advantages to prevent destructive policy updates. This enables stable policy improvement without backpropagating gradients through the world model.

captions.F9: Real-world hardware setup used in experiments. Visible are the ARX AC One dual-arm robot, the overhead base camera, wrist cameras on both arms, and a total of four Xense optical tactile sensors mounted on the fingertip grippers.

takeaways: Treating tactile images and marker displacement vectors directly as image patches for a large pretrained video VAE and Transformer captures far stronger priors than training separate tactile encoders.

In world model evaluation, low-level reconstruction metrics like PSNR or FID do not guarantee reliable task outcome predictions (semantic fidelity); explicit task outcome consistency losses are essential.

With an accurate, visuo-tactile consistent world model, a physical robot's task success rate can be significantly enhanced purely through imagined trial-and-error (GRPO) without a single hardware trial.
limitations: Requires collecting annotated data and training separate task outcome and scene reward models before post-training can take place.
Evaluations are currently limited to four dual-arm tasks; zero-shot generalization to longer multi-stage horizons or vastly different sensor shapes and contact areas remains untested.

Imagined reinforcement learning benefits vary depending on baseline policy expressiveness and task difficulty—for instance, the Flow Matching policy failed to improve from 0% success on test tube insertion and Rubik's cube manipulation.
